opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it came down to looking at where our customers were actually getting stuck. When we talked to enterprises, almost nobody said, "The problem is that the base model isn't smart enough." The models are already incredibly capable in a general sense. What people struggled with was everything around the model: How do I connect it to my data? How do I know if it's giving the right answer for *my* domain? How do I govern it, monitor it, and improve it over time? How do I get from a cool demo to something I'd actually put in front of customers or use to make business decisions?

So we asked where we could add the most value. Training a general frontier model is an enormous, capital-intensive race, and several very good labs are already running it. The marginal benefit of us being one more competitor there seemed much lower than solving the problems that sit between a great model and a working application.

There's also a research angle I care a lot about. A lot of the progress in what you can actually do with AI comes from systems, not just bigger models. You combine models with retrieval, tools, multiple calls, verification steps, and you optimize the whole pipeline for a specific task. That compound AI systems view is where I think a lot of the quality gains are for real applications. Something like a domain-specific agent that's well evaluated and tuned on a company's own data will often beat a raw frontier model on that task, even if the underlying model is smaller or cheaper.

And it plays to what Databricks is good at. Our customers' data already lives on the platform, along with the governance, lineage, and pipelines. So the natural thing for us is to make that the best place to build AI that actually works on your data: evaluation, tuning, and tooling to build agents and measure their quality. We want to be model-agnostic too. Use whichever model is best, whether it's open or from one of the labs, and we help you make it useful.

The way I'd summarize it: the bottleneck has shifted from "Can the model do this in principle?" to "Can I trust this system to do it reliably in my setting?" That second question is the one we decided to focus on.

r001.rationale: The response says several labs are already training frontier models, but does not state that an expected abundance of models from others is a reason to focus on usefulness.

r002.rationale: It contrasts frontier-model training with building application systems using retrieval, tools, verification, evaluation, and tuning to make models work reliably for specific tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it came from looking at what our customers were actually struggling with. We work with thousands of enterprises, and when we talked to them, almost none of them were blocked on model quality in the abstract. They were blocked on getting a model to work well on their specific problem, with their specific data, in their specific context. The hard part wasn't "is GPT-4 smart enough?" It was "how do I get this thing to reliably answer questions about my internal documents, or my product catalog, or my support tickets, and not make stuff up, and do it at a cost that makes sense."

And when you look at that problem, a general frontier model is only one piece of it. You need retrieval, you need evaluation, you need a way to iterate on prompts and pipelines, you need governance over what data the model sees, you need to be able to fine-tune or adapt things when the base model isn't good enough. That whole surrounding system is where most of the engineering effort goes, and it's where most of the value gets created or lost. So it felt like the highest-leverage place for us to focus.

There's also a strategic angle. Training a frontier model from scratch is enormously expensive, and there are already several very well-funded labs doing it, and competing on exactly that axis didn't seem like the best use of our resources. What we care about is that enterprises can use the best model for their task, whether that's an open model, something from OpenAI or Anthropic, or a model they've trained themselves. Being neutral there is actually a feature for us. If we had our own frontier model, we'd have an incentive to push people toward it even when it wasn't the right choice.

That said, we didn't completely stay out of training. We did DBRX, and a lot of the fine-tuning and pretraining work we do with customers. But the motivation there was different. It was partly to show that you can train a very capable model on this platform, and partly because we learned a lot about what it takes to build the data pipelines and training infrastructure, which then flows back into the product. The goal was never "beat the frontier labs on benchmarks." It was "make it easy for an organization to take a model, adapt it to what they actually need, and measure whether it's working."

And honestly, I think the most interesting research questions right now are in that space too. Things like how do you build systems that combine multiple models and tools, how do you do evaluation when there's no single right answer, how do you get the system to improve from feedback without a huge labeling effort. That's a lot of what we've been working on, both at Databricks and in my academic group. It's a really rich area, and it's one where I think the gap between what's possible and what people have actually deployed is still enormous.

r001.rationale: The response points to several well-funded labs training frontier models and says enterprises should be able to choose among open models and models from OpenAI or Anthropic, supporting Databricks’ focus on making models useful.

r002.rationale: It describes usefulness as requiring a surrounding system—retrieval, evaluation, iteration, governance, and adaptation—and contrasts that work with training a frontier model from scratch.

astra-6.text:
Well, for us, the starting point is what customers actually want to do with AI. They’re usually trying to solve a particular problem using their own data, within constraints around cost, latency, and reliability. A more capable general model can help, but it doesn’t solve that whole problem by itself.

There’s a lot of work in connecting a model to the right information, evaluating whether it’s doing the task correctly, and improving the system based on those results. That’s a very natural focus for Databricks because we’re already helping people manage and work with their data.

And training models can absolutely be part of that. But the objective is to make the application work well. You might get there with a smaller, specialized model, better retrieval, or a combination of models and tools. We want to help customers figure out which approach actually delivers value.

r001.rationale: The response says a more capable model can help but is not enough; it does not identify an expected abundance of models from others as a reason for Databricks’ focus.

r002.rationale: The response describes connecting models to information, evaluating them, and improving the system, and says the objective is a working application rather than model training alone.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, the starting point was what our customers actually wanted to do with AI. They have their own data, their own business processes, and specific problems they want to solve. A more capable general model helps, but it doesn’t automatically give you a system that can use that data reliably or that you can evaluate and improve.

So we focused on the whole system: how you connect models to your data, how you measure whether they’re doing the right thing, and how you make them efficient enough to deploy. Sometimes that means training or fine-tuning a model; sometimes it means retrieval or combining several components. We thought there was a lot of value in making those pieces work together and giving customers control over the result.

r001.rationale: The response says a more capable general model helps, but does not cite an expected abundance of models from others as a reason for Databricks’ focus.

r002.rationale: It describes making models useful as building and coordinating a whole system around data, evaluation, and deployment, rather than simply training a general frontier model.
